blocks.title: Half-life
blocks.text: The half-life, t1/2, is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half of its original value.

Calculating k by the half-life method means measuring the time for the concentration of a reactant to halve. For a first-order reaction the rate constant and the half-life are related by k = 0.693 / t1/2. A sample of hydrogen peroxide decomposing by a first-order reaction has a half-life of 2 hours: convert to seconds, 2 x 60 x 60 = 7200 s, then k = 0.693 / 7200 = 9.6 x 10^-5 s-1. Sample Problem 7.2: the first-order conversion of cyclopropane to propene has a half-life of 17.0 min; convert to seconds, 17 x 60 = 1020 s, then k = 0.693 / 1020 = 6.79 x 10^-4 s-1 (the print writes the units as dm3 mol-1 s-1, which belong to second order).

blocks.alt: Left: a two-step pipeline for the NO and H2 reaction, a thick red slow arrow from 2NO + H2 to N2 + H2O2 and a thin green fast arrow from H2O2 + H2 to 2H2O, with notes on intermediates, the NO2 and F2 mechanism and molecularity. Right: a purple decay curve of concentration against time with dashed lines at c0/2, c0/4 and c0/8 marking successive half-lives.
blocks.caption: A two-step mechanism with its rate-determining step, and the half-life of a first-order reaction (original diagram after topic 7.6 and the half-life examples of 7.5.2).
blocks.long_description: The slow first step controls the rate, so the rate law contains only its reactants, 2NO and H2, while the intermediate H2O2 is made and consumed and never appears in the overall equation. In a first-order decay the concentration halves in every half-life whatever its starting value, so k = 0.693 divided by the half-life: 6.8 x 10^-4 s-1 for cyclopropane with a half-life of 17 minutes.

blocks.prompt: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 15 minutes and an initial concentration of 0.100 mol dm-3. Find k, and the time for the concentration to fall to 0.0125 mol dm-3.
blocks.explanation: k = 0.693 / (15 x 60) = 0.693 / 900 = 7.7 x 10^-4 s-1 (0.046 min-1). From 0.100 to 0.0125 is three halvings (0.050, 0.025, 0.0125), so 3 x 15 = 45 minutes; the initial concentration does not affect k.

items: Half-life: time for a reactant to halve; first order: k = 0.693 / t1/2 (H2O2, 2 h = 7200 s, k = 9.6 x 10^-5 s-1; cyclopropane, 17 min, k = 6.79 x 10^-4 s-1).
